question:
Let $f(x) = |x - 2| + |x + 1|$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$.

(a) Discuss the continuity and differentiability of $f(x)$ at the points $x = -1$ and $x = 2$.

(b) Determine $f'(x)$ for all $x$.
explanation:
(a) The function $f(x)$ has non-differentiable points where the expressions inside the modulus change sign, i.e., at $x = -1$ and $x = 2$.

First, check continuity at $x = -1$:

$\lim_{x \to -1^-} f(x) = |-1 - 2| + |-1 + 1| = | -3| + |0| = 3 + 0 = 3$

$\lim_{x \to -1^+} f(x) = | (-1 +) - 2| + |(-1 +) + 1|$
For $x > -1$, $x + 1 > 0$ and $x - 2 < 0$ if $x < 2$.
So:
$|x - 2| + |x + 1| = -(x - 2) + (x + 1) = -x + 2 + x + 1 = 3$
So both one-sided limits and $f(-1) = 3$. So $f(x)$ is continuous at $x = -1$.

Similarly, at $x = 2$:
For $x < 2$, $x-2 < 0$, $x + 1 > 0$ ($x > -1$)
$|x-2| + |x+1| = -(x - 2) + (x + 1) = -x + 2 + x + 1 = 3$
For $x > 2$, $x-2 > 0$, $x + 1 > 0$
$|x-2| + |x+1| = (x - 2) + (x + 1) = 2x - 1$
Check limits:
$\lim_{x \to 2^-} f(x) = 3$
$\lim_{x \to 2^+} f(x) = 2*2 - 1 = 3$
And $f(2) = |2-2| + |2+1| = 0 + 3 = 3$
So $f(x)$ is continuous at $x = 2$.

Now check differentiability at the points:

Compute left and right derivatives at $x = -1$:
For $x < -1$, both expressions are negative: $|x-2| = -(x-2)$, $|x+1| = -(x+1)$
So $f(x) = -(x-2) - (x+1) = -x+2-x-1 = -2x + 1$
$\implies f'(x) = -2$ for $x < -1$
For $x > -1$, $x+1 > 0$, $x-2 < 0$: $f(x) = -x + 2 + x + 1 = 3$, so $f'(x) = 0$
Thus, $LHD$ at $x = -1$: $= -2$, $RHD = 0$.
So not differentiable at $x = -1$.

At $x = 2$:
For $x < 2$, as above, $f'(x) = 0$
For $x > 2$, both positive: $f(x) = (x-2) + (x+1) = 2x - 1, f'(x) = 2$
So left-hand derivative at 2: $0$, right-hand derivative $2$
So $f(x)$ is not differentiable at $x = 2$.

(b) Full derivative:
For $x < -1$: $f(x) = -2x + 1$, $f'(x) = -2$
For $-1 < x < 2$: $f(x) = 3$, $f'(x) = 0$
For $x > 2$: $f(x) = 2x - 1$, $f'(x) = 2$
$f'(x) = \begin{cases} -2, & x < -1 \\ 0, & -1 < x < 2 \\ 2, & x > 2 \end{cases}$, not defined at $x = -1, 2$.

options.A:
(a) $f(x)$ is continuous at $x=-1$ and $x=2$, but not differentiable at both points.
(b) $f'(x)=\begin{cases}-2, & x<-1 \\ 0, & -12\end{cases}$, and $f'(x)$ is not defined at $x=-1,2$.
options.B:
(a) $f(x)$ is discontinuous at $x=-1$ and continuous at $x=2$.
(b) $f'(x)=\begin{cases}0, & x<-1 \\ 2, & -12\end{cases}$.
options.C:
(a) $f(x)$ is continuous and differentiable at both $x=-1$ and $x=2$.
(b) $f'(x)=2$ for all real $x$.
options.D:
(a) $f(x)$ is not continuous at both $x=-1$ and $x=2$.
(b) $f'(x)$ is undefined for all $x$.
